segments.text: Hello and welcome to The Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, so-called environmentally sound, green textiles, are some of them actually woven over the damaged lives of the workers who produce them.
Protecting children's brains from the toxic effects of poverty. Important findings for women with breast cancer that could save them from unnecessary treatment.
Important findings for people who've been treated for bowel cancer, which could save them a whole lot of anxiety and time.
When you buy a piece of clothing that has viscose or rayon in it, or when you see some cellophane
wrapping, you should spare a thought for the people who've been involved in the manufacture
of the raw material. According to a new book, there's a huge burden of serious brain and heart
damage among workers in the manufacturing process, which has been known for over 100 years and
persists to this day, even in rich nations. The book's called Fake Silk, the Lethal History of
viscose rayon, and it's by Paul Blank, who's professor of medicine at the University of
California, San Francisco, and chief of UCSF's Division of Occupational and Environmental Medicine.
Viscose has been used for a lot of things, not just textiles, but rayon is viscose turned into
thread and then turned into synthetic cellulose-based textile. It was really the very first
synthetic textile. But the exact same chemistry leads to cellophane. And what people probably
don't realize is a lot of the synthetic sponges that we use every day are mostly viscose as well.
And then there's some other specialty uses, such as viscose film casings for sausage,
what we like to call in America skinless weenies.
Kind of a harmless phrase for something that his manufacturer, you say, is incredibly toxic.
So essentially, chemistry goes back to the 18th and 19th centuries.
That's right. The chemistry of viscose goes back to the very end of the 19th century, turn of the 20th century.
The main toxic chemical involved, which is called carbon disulfide, was actually before that a very big chemical in the rubber industry.
And carbon disulfide, they first of all didn't know what to do with it, but then it became very obvious that it was a really useful solvent to dissolve other stuff.

Yes, it's incredible solvent. It's very special. And that's why it's really been only carbon disulfide that's worked in this viscose process. There's an alternative chemical that's been developed in the last couple of decades that's not very widely used, but basically the name of the game has been carbon disulfide.
So to make viscose, to make rayon, take us through the process. What happens?
It's a pretty simple process. What you do is you take wood pulp or some other source of cellulose,
grind it up, bleach it, and then you add caustic to it, let it sit around for a while. Then you
put into it carbon disulfide and it turns it into this yellowy toxic syrup that you force through
tubes into a bath of sulfuric acid. And then the cellulose is regenerated as thread or you
regenerated as the thin film. And that's the process. And what happens is it's pure cellulose
again. The carbon disulfide flies off. Unfortunately, it flies off into the air that the workers are
breathing unless you take special precautions, which most of the time they didn't.
And this, of course, cellulose has been reinvented as a natural fiber that's harmless,
which in fact it is once it's reconstituted.
That's correct. And it's being marketed as a green product. I like to call it greenwashing
because it's really quite cynical.
They like to even push that theme harder
if instead of wood pulp from trees, they use bamboo.
It's, you know, the poster child for renewable.
So when you wear clothes that have been reconstituted from bamboo,
this is the process we're talking about by and large.
Absolutely.
Even now in the 21st century.
Oh, yeah.
So take us through the history then of how it's affected workers.
The very first toxic effect was it drove workers insane.
They would develop acute psychosis. There was a famous rubber factory in the 19th century that
had iron bars on its second story window because the workers were so prone to jump out and kill
themselves. You're kidding. No, I'm not making this up. And through the 20th century, there were
multiple reports of insanity, people killing themselves, people killing other people,
mostly in the viscous rayon industry, but there were other sources of exposure too.
It was used in the United States. I don't know about Australia, but in the United States, it was the preferred gopher poison.
You would put it down gopher holes because it's heavier than air and kill gophers.
And there was a report of these two brothers who had a 20-gallon can of this stuff and was leaking unbeknownst to them.
And one of them went completely crazy and murdered somebody and then killed himself.
These stories just kind of are out there in the literature.
Now, did the employers of these people recognize that this was an industrial problem?
What was the response to this clear association between the manufacturing process and people developing psychosis?
Well, there was a kind of split.
When RAND came to be marketed, they basically tried to forget all the things that had been learned from the same chemical in the rubber industry.
I can't prove that they depressed knowledge, but there certainly was no impetus to publish very much of anything.
The big centers, biggest of them being Great Britain at the time, didn't publish any information at all.
And it went for another two decades before it started being published.
When the first big study was done systematically in the United States in the 1930s, the late 1930s,
they found that about 30% of the working population exposed demonstrated pretty severe effect.
And it wasn't just neurological, it was cardiovascular as well, affected the heart.
Well, that was only able to be shown much later
because the techniques to show an increased death rate
from heart attack and stroke are much more sophisticated.
It was really the 1960s.
That is an example where there is a smoking gun
where you can show that Courtauld did everything that it could
to keep those data from being published in Great Britain.
So there were no whistleblowers at that time,
no doctors who were saying,
I'm seeing this, why aren't you doing something about it?
There was no noise?
There were doctors and other people agitating, but in fact, it's not so easy to get the word out.
But there were articles would appear in big journals and in newspapers, and then everything would be forgotten again.
So there was no response in terms of industrial hygiene, better ventilation, isolating the mix so that the vapor doesn't come off or trying to prevent the vapor coming off?
There were some efforts, but in fact, there was always resistance or reluctance to accept that the levels which were purported to be safe were not safe.
So even when they would reduce levels, that was still way too high.
That's still reflected in the standard in the United States where the legal limit is 20 parts per million.

So the standard in the United States is still legally 20 parts per million, even though the United States Research Agency has recommended that the level be significantly lower than that, one part per million, 20 times more protective.
World War II is where rayon really took off.
Well, it took off before that, in fact, because in the Depression, despite worldwide economic collapse, the rayon industry was really growing logarithmically.
And that just continued through the war where it was a strategic materiel.
But even before that, it was very big business, not just in Britain, the United States, Germany, Italy, Japan, but we're all huge producers.
Official German policy actually was to mix rayon into other fabrics.
And that's what we have today.
When you buy something that'll say 20% viscose, that's the typical kinds of viscose blends that we have nowadays.
And that actually led to higher exposure in the workers because the technology was they would pull this long bunch of threads called a tow dripping with carbon disulfide out of the vat.
People got even more exposure that way.
And then in the war in occupied Europe, the Germans really manufactured their rayon with slave labor across the continent.
And you found one factory that was only eight kilometers from Theresienstadt, the concentration camp.

That's correct, but there were other factories, and we have records because one of the important French resistance fighters, a woman who was arrested very early in the occupation, was sent as a slave laborer to one of the other German factories, and after the war wrote a memoir for experiences.
Of course, she didn't know what she was working with, only that it made her blind and burned her fingers.
Now, we're still producing rayon today, but in developing countries.

Rayon as fiber is in China and Indonesia and India. We know almost nothing about the conditions, particularly in Indonesia and India, although we have a sense from limited reports that it's not very good. But it's important to remember that other viscose products are produced still in Europe and North America and elsewhere. But the textile business has largely gone to those countries. And Thailand, I think, is a producer as well.
Is your suspicion then that when you wear something that's got viscose in it, it could be built on the power of a 30% rate of disability from toxicity due to carbon disulfide?
It may not be that high anymore, although who knows what it is in these factories in India.
I would say largely yes when you buy that shirt for $12 in the warehouse store that should really cost three times that amount.
But the reason you got it so cheaply is that some unfortunate in a 15th floor death trap walk up in Bangladesh made it for 10 cents a day.
It's no risk to you from wearing that shirt.
And the same thing with anything made of rat.
You obviously wrote this book with a sense of outrage.
Has there been litigation?
Has DuPont, Courtaulds or whatever Courtaulds has become since then, have they suffered litigation as a result of this?
In the United States, you can't sue your employer.
The workers' compensation system in the United States precludes suing your employer.
In Great Britain, they have a system where a disease has to be officially recognized
in order to be easily compensatable.
And although certain effects of carbon disulfide are recognized in Great Britain,
they never did recognize heart attack as being potentially related,
despite the epidemiologic evidence that was quite convincing.
So what's the lesson?

Well, I mean, one lesson is that knowledge is power and that when a brand new product comes on the market, like Rayon was such a highfalutin new product at the time, we should think about what is behind that technology.
What are the risks and what are the benefits and who's getting the benefits and who suffers the risk?
And in terms of industrial safety?
In terms of industrial safety, I think it's an ongoing struggle that has not particularly progressed in the last 100 years the way one might have hoped.
Just broadening it out, and finally, my question is related to problems that affect just workers in an industry or problems that escape to the general community.
And it strikes me that asbestos, because it escaped to the general community, got a lot of attention.
do we still have an issue where it's just the worker who gets affected rather than the general
community where it tends to be buried still versus toxins which escape if you like into the general
environment and affect the general community that we have if you like a double standard i think
you're absolutely correct that is very much the case paul blank is professor of medicine at the
university of california san francisco and chief of ucsf's division of occupational and environmental
medicine. The book's called Fake Silk, The Lethal History of Viscose Rain, and the publisher is Yale
University Press. You're listening to The Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio and CBC Radio
across Canada. Two reviews of the latest evidence on early breast cancer and people who've been
treated for bowel cancer, which hasn't yet spread, have good news. A lot of time, inconvenience,
expense and anxiety could be saved. An author on both of these reviews was Bridget Hickey,
a radiation oncologist at Princess Alexandra Hospital in Brisbane.
Let's start with women who just have the lump removed
and need radiation therapy afterwards.
The debate is over how many fractions they need,
how many sessions of radiotherapy.
What we did was searched extensively the literature,
published and unpublished around the world,
according to the principles of the Cochrane Collaboration Methodology.
To explain here, we're talking about a systematic review
where you take all the evidence and you stir it up, remix it, reanalyse it to see where the balance
lies of evidence. That's right. And the question was, is using fewer treatments as good as using
the standard 25 to 30 treatments as good in terms of breast cancer outcomes, survival,
and the cosmetic outcome? Because remember that breast conservation is all about the cosmetic
outcome. And just forgive me if I'm missing something here. I'd have thought that fewer
fractions would have no impact on the cosmetic result. Why would you expect less radiotherapy
to make the breast look any different? Yeah, that's to do with the dose per fraction.
If you're hypofractionating, you give a bigger dose per fraction that can be associated with
more late effects on slow reacting tissues that cause more fibrosis and more scarring.
So essentially what we're talking about here is that you get a certain dose, if you like,
in total of your radiation therapy over a period of five or six weeks.
And the idea is you get kind of the same dose,
but in a much shorter period of time.
Roughly the same dose, yeah.
Which means that each zap is going to be stronger.
That's right.
Okay, so you looked at all the available evidence from randomised trials.
What did you find?
Well, we looked at over 8,000 women in known studies,
and we found that there's no difference in local control
or cosmetic outcome, overall survival,
or breast cancer specific or relapse-free survival
so that the outcomes that matter to the doctors
who want to control the cancer and the patients,
there's no difference.
So it's as safe.
And the woman has been less inconvenienced
because she hasn't had to turn up
in a radiation therapy department so often.
And how many days does this save?
Conventional treatment would be 25 to 30 treatments,
but with hyperfractionation, five treatments a week.
So that's five or six weeks and hyperfractionated?
Would be 15 to 16 treatments.
So just over three weeks.
You can imagine for busy women who are working with children, it's a great saving in terms of
their time. We know that if you live a long way from a radiation therapy department, you may be
more likely to choose mastectomy based on the fact that you don't want to be away from your family
and you work for six weeks. And then, you know, it saves money, time, resources, and can mean that
we can treat more patients. So some women choose mastectomy because they can't deal with the
inconvenience of the radiotherapy. Yeah, that's right. Before you have all your colleagues not
talking to anyone anymore. We pay, apart from the public sector and the private sector,
they get paid per fraction. So they're going to get paid less if they don't do hypofractionated.
So there must be quite significant disincentives to actually do this because people are going to
lose money. Changing practice is difficult. There has been more adoption of hypofractionation. And
in fact, it's one of the big moves in radiation oncology at the moment is the move towards
hypofractionation, not only in breast cancer, also in prostate cancer. And I think now we can say
with the results of this review that really it's just as good and just as safe. People had a
theoretical concern that using larger doses per fraction when the heart vessels were irradiated
might be associated with increased cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. But these days we've got
more techniques that we can use to actually avoid irradiating the heart. So that takes out that
argument. And so is there evidence that in the private sector you're more likely to get the
longer course than the short course? I'm not aware of evidence. But really the message here for women
when they're being referred for radiation oncology, whether it's the public or private sector,
is ask for hypofractionated in the shortest course that's got the evidence behind it.
At least discuss it. For some women with large breasts, we're concerned about using hypofractionated
technique because there might be more late toxicity. But we can again deal with that by
other techniques such as treating women lying on their stomach and that reduces the dimension of
the breast and makes it more possible to use hypofractionation. Now the second Cochrane review
you've just been involved with involves follow-up of people who've been treated for colorectal
cancer, in other words bowel cancer, which hasn't spread. So it's a common cancer, one of the
commonest. And of course a lot of our outpatient resources are taken up with people with follow-up
And that means that new people with a new problem that need to be diagnosed don't get in to see doctors because they're crammed with follow-up.
And so you've been looking at really what sort of follow-up people need after a potentially curative surgery for bowel cancer.
Absolutely.
The genesis of this review was when I was working in New Zealand.
And as you know, New Zealand and Australia have got the highest incidence of colorectal cancer in the world.
And we were understaffed and we were seeing so many people and we wondered whether we were actually benefiting them.
And when we recognised there was some controversy about that, we did this review.
We didn't so much examine what the perfect follow-up regimen involves.
What we looked at was, does intensive follow-up,
is it better than less intense follow-up in terms of survival?
And so what's intensive?
In the studies involved, it varied from some versus none
to very intensive follow-up with lots of scans and MRIs and CTs.
And so what did you find?
Well, we were quite shocked because the latest iteration of this review, we don't find that there is any improvement in survival.
In fact, there is no difference in overall survival between the two study arms.
Colorectal cancer-specific survival is the same, and so is relapse-free survival.
You do more salvage operations, and you find fewer recurrences outside the setting of the clinic visit, but the survival is the same.
so that's put what we know turned on its head which is a little bit confronting
I suppose both reviews have got the theme that more is not always better. So somebody's listening
to this who's had a bowel cancer removed it hasn't spread have you landed on what is the
sweet point for follow-up? I have to say we haven't that really was not something we were
able to tease out of the data. So just give me the middle ground then in this study if people
it was very different and so on. I mean, was it every three months you get a colonoscopy or once
a year you come back and we do an MRI scan or we just do a rectal examination or feel your tummy?
What was kind of the middle ground? Kind of the middle ground was probably a CT once a year,
colonoscopy once a year, CT looking at lungs and liver and blood tests looking at use of a marker
called CEA. We weren't able to demonstrate that the use of tumour markers improved survival.
And these studies spanned a long time interval so that over that time things have changed, investigations have become more sophisticated and the surgery has become more sophisticated.

So we wondered whether we'd got better at doing the operations to remove, for example, a solitary liver metastasis and post-operative care had got better, but we weren't able to demonstrate any difference looking by study age.
So it was a very robust result.
We've always known there's a population of patients who have a solitary liver metastasis,
for example, diagnosed.
If they have it excised, they have a long survival.
And that's been reported and known for a long time.
But without doing a randomised control trial, you don't know whether those patients just
had indolent disease and they would have been OK without it being removed.
The other thing that might be happening now is that we have more effective systemic treatments
when you do have metastatic disease.
and that might be narrowing the gap
so that if you do have metastatic disease diagnosed,
you have better survival
because there's more effective chemotherapy.
So in other words, the implication of that
is that if you have a less intensive regime
and the tumour does come back in between times,
the treatment is better.
That's possible.
Or it makes no difference at all
and you might as well just wait the year
and get the CT scan.
Yeah.
But obviously what needs to happen now
is studies need to be done
to work out what is the optimal regime.
Yeah.
It's a mess.
Yeah.
So Bridget, knowing what you know now, if you were unfortunate enough to develop an uncomplicated bowel cancer, you had curative surgery, what would you want to have done to you as follow-up?
Great question. I'd probably still have a CT scan once a year.
Just to keep yourself comfortable.
Well, it would probably make me very anxious.
And that's the other problem, is the more you do, the more anxiety there is.
There's a word for it, scan anxiety, scan anxiety.
One of the things we wanted to look at in this view was the harms of follow-up,
because every day I see patients who come and see me wound up anxious
because they're coming to see me and am I going to find a recurrence?
And we've got to know that we're benefiting people in order to put them through that.
Thank you very much indeed.
Thank you.
Bridget Hickey is a radiation oncologist at Princess Alexandra Hospital in Brisbane.
There are many factors that affect children's development,
from the genes they inherit from their parents,
the age of their father at conception, and their environment, especially if there's poverty.
Poverty is well known to be toxic to children.
A study in the southern United States where they have the worst poverty in the nation
has looked at the brain scans of young people who've spent years growing up in deprivation
to see if a parenting program made any difference.
One of the researchers was Gene Brody from the Centre for Family Research at the University of Georgia, Athens.
Economic hardship really ripped the psychological fabric of the parents rearing children.
These parents worked very hard, despite living in tough circumstances, to do their best.
But the chronic day-to-day stressors associated with poverty made them feel badly.
And for some children, this had the consequence of them not doing as well as they could
of reaching their potential in school and other areas. And this jived with other research from
around the world, actually, that shows that children growing up in poverty conditions
where resources are scarce, but stressors are plenty, tend not to develop as well academically
and socially as children who aren't battling these particular kinds of stressors.
And you had some evidence that the brains were in fact different.
You know, there were clues there where researchers would associate living in poverty with diminished brain development.

And it made us wonder, since we follow children from pre-adolescence through young adulthood, whether children who spent more years living in poverty would have smaller brain volume in areas of the brain that were important for their academic development, for their memory, and for their ability to cope with stress.
And unfortunately, we found it was.
And which parts...
For some children.
And which parts of the brain, and what sort of functionality?
The parts of the brain that we focused on were the hippocampus and the amygdala.
So that's memory, emotional control, that sort of thing?
Right, yes.
Now you also looked at an intervention called Strong African American Families, which was, what, a parenting program?
Yeah. In 2001, 2002, we developed a program for African-American families living in the rural
South that was designed to mitigate stress by enhancing the quality of caregiving that children
received. And we have studied the effectiveness of this program to promote psychological adjustment,
academic achievement, and some health outcomes as well. And that caused us to wonder if the
benefits of this program would extend to brain development. Would youth who at age 11 live more
years in poverty and whose brain development was assessed at age 25 not show the deleterious
effects of poverty if they had participated and received enhanced levels of parenting that were
taught by the Strong African American Families Program. And what did you find? We were delighted
to find it did, so that the association or the link between poverty and diminished brain development
was found only for children who did not participate in the prevention program.
And what were the elements of this program?
What were you teaching parents to do?
Because you probably know in Australia we've developed one particular parenting program,
which is quite popular internationally.
What were you doing with these parents?
What were you teaching them?
First, I want to give a shout out to Professor Matt Sanders.
At Griffith University.
whose prevention programs are internationally known.
Our program was a little different than Professor Sanders
in that the rural southern context that our participants grew up in are unique.
And the parenting practices that are successful in the Black Belt
might be different than parenting practices in the northern parts of the United States
or in very urban areas.
So we spent 10 years documenting what were the parenting processes
that enhanced the development of children in the rural South.
And we settled on and focused on a few things that really tended to matter.
And these things were providing emotional support for children,
increase the amount of time that parents spend with their children, increase the use of a parenting dynamic
which involves high levels of control laced with high levels of warmth.
The kids know that the reason their parents are keeping them in tow and being very vigilant about their children
is that they often live in some dangerous circumstances which require that protection.
Another thing we did was to enhance how routinized the home environments were.
So making them less chaotic.
Making them much less chaotic, much more predictable,
making sure there was a time and place for them to do their studies,
and all the while increasing their presence at their children's school.
One of the things that we find is the more that home environments are routinized and predictable
and parents show up at school, schools treat the parents differently,
and in turn the children benefit more from the teacher's attention at school.
and over time this particular formulation of parenting practices
really has been shown to aid not only psychosocial development
but health and now it appears to expand into the brain.
And just finally, Gene Brody, the applicability to other areas?
This program has now been disseminated into 40 communities across the United States
and we are optimistic about its ability to continue to enhance the development of African-American youth
and time will tell.
Thanks for joining us on The Health Report.
Glad to be here. Thank you for asking me.
Jean Brodie is the Director of the Centre for Family Research at the University of Georgia, Athens.
You've been listening to The Health Report. I'm Norman Swan.
I hope you'll join me next week.
